title: AGST 50104 Syllabus
text:
AGST 50104


The course develops the ability to choose experimental designs, formulate fixed- and random-effect models, conduct ANOVA and mixed-model analyses, evaluate assumptions, and communicate results in agricultural and biological research.


By the end of the course, students should be able to:

Apply replication, randomization, and blocking to plan valid experiments.
Select an appropriate CRD, RCBD, factorial, split-plot, or incomplete-block design.
Translate research hypotheses into models with correctly specified fixed and random effects.
Conduct ANOVA, linear mixed-model, and generalized linear-model analyses with appropriate diagnostics.
Distinguish statistical significance from practical importance and communicate the results.
Recognize pseudoreplication, confounding, and incorrect error terms.

The KAI Inventory focuses on preferred problem-solving style—especially how a person approaches structure and change. It does not measure intelligence, ability, or creativity level.




My result

36StructureRule/Group Conformity





What I take from this result
My score is most useful as a prompt for understanding how I work with other people. I tend to combine disciplined execution with independent analysis: I appreciate structure when it improves clarity, but I am comfortable revisiting assumptions and proposing a different route when the evidence supports it.
The three component scores describe different aspects of that preference. They should be interpreted together and in context, rather than as separate measures of performance.

The supplied slide decks contain 452 slides across six chapters. This index records their conceptual scope without redistributing copyrighted slide content. The Fall 2026 syllabus assigns Chapters 2–6 to Exam I; Chapter 1 remains a course foundation.


CH 01 · 58 SLIDES ### Biochemistry and the unity of life Chemical foundations, cellular organization, evolution, energy, and the molecular logic of living systems.

CH 05 · 71 SLIDES ### Genes and genomes Restriction enzymes, sequencing, PCR, cloning, expression analysis, genome editing, transgenic models, and gene therapy.

title: Chapter 10: Renewable Energy
text:
What you will learn

Explain how solar, wind, water, geothermal and biomass systems supply useful energy.
Distinguish resource renewal, carbon performance and ecological impact.
Calculate energy, capacity factor and a simple storage balance.
Defend a transition plan with a safeguard, a stress test and explicit limitations.

Reading: the complete Chapter 10 in the supplied chapter PDF: Science (printed pp. 298–309), Issues (310–317), Solutions (317–325), summary and review (326–327).
Bring from Chapter 9: energy is an amount; power is a rate; an energy carrier is not the same as a primary resource; and a useful comparison follows a consistent service and life-cycle boundary. The experiments here use fictional data so you can isolate mechanisms. They do not predict the performance of a real community or product.

title: Chapter 10: Renewable Energy
text:
The chapter at a glance
Central question: Can we develop renewable energy resources to help sustain a thriving economy without adversely affecting the environment? [Book, p. 297.]









Science
Issues
Solutions
Takeaway




Solar, wind, water, geothermal heat and biomass follow different conversion pathways.
Land, wildlife, rivers, food systems, material needs and the timing of supply remain important.
Improve siting and operation, protect ecological flows, choose feedstocks carefully and integrate demand, generation and storage.
Renewable describes resource renewal—not an absence of impacts. Evaluate a complete system in its setting.



This complete lesson follows all eleven numbered sections of Chapter 10. It is a self-paced chapter course, not a transcript constrained to 50 minutes. The separate presentation summarizes the central question, mechanisms, issues, solutions and takeaways for a 50-minute class.
The opening Samsø example asks us to think about a community’s energy portfolio and participation, not one device. An annual renewable-energy balance is not proof of an isolated system meeting every instant of demand. State the boundary: electricity or all energy, annual totals or hourly service, and local generation or exchange with a wider grid. Treat the book’s account as a historical case. [Book, pp. 296–297.]

Science · One label, different mechanisms

10.1 Solar energy can be used as a heat source and to generate electricity
Solar energy can supply a service directly as heat or be converted into electricity. A building that admits winter sunlight and limits summer heat gain uses design to manage energy flows. A solar-water-heating system transfers absorbed energy to water or another fluid. Neither requires electricity generation as an intermediate step.
Photovoltaic (PV) cells absorb light in a semiconductor. The energy of absorbed photons can free charge carriers, and the device’s internal electric field helps separate them; a connected external circuit delivers electrical energy. This is not a miniature steam engine. Clouds can reduce available light without making output necessarily zero, because diffuse sunlight can still reach a panel. Device temperature, shading and the system configuration also matter. [Book, pp. 298–301; DOE photovoltaic-cell basics.]


Photovoltaics: light to electricity





Reconstructed illustration adapted from Molles & Borrell, Environment: Science, Issues, Solutions (2016), Fig. 10.7, in §10.1. The drawing simplifies a silicon cell. DOE photovoltaic-cell explanation.

Enlarge figure


Absorb lightAbsorbed photons transfer energy to charge carriers in the semiconductor.


Separate chargesThe junction helps separate charge carriers so the illuminated cell can supply a voltage.


Deliver electrical energyA connected circuit allows current to flow through a load. No boiling water or turbine is involved.



The moving outline guides attention; it does not measure energy, fluid speed or system performance. Use the experiments for numerical comparisons.


Concentrating solar power (CSP) uses mirrors to concentrate sunlight as heat. A heated fluid supports a thermal cycle that can drive a turbine and generator. Some designs store thermal energy for later use. Distinguish the collection of sunlight, the storage of heat and the generation of electricity: these are separate functions. A statement about cooling water at a thermal plant should not automatically be applied to a rooftop PV panel.


Concentrating solar power: sunlight becomes heat





Reconstructed illustration adapted from Molles & Borrell, Environment: Science, Issues, Solutions (2016), Fig. 10.6 and §10.8. This is one conceptual tower-and-storage arrangement; not every CSP plant uses salt storage.

Enlarge figure


Concentrate sunlightMirrors direct sunlight to a receiver, where its energy heats a fluid.


Store or transfer heatIn the illustrated arrangement, heated salt stores thermal energy and transfers heat to a separate power cycle.


Run a thermal power cycleSteam drives a turbine and generator, then condenses. Storage shifts heat use in time but does not create energy.



The moving outline guides attention; it does not measure energy, fluid speed or system performance. Use the experiments for numerical comparisons.


Check: classify solar hot water, a PV-powered lamp and a mirror-based thermal power station. The services and conversion steps are different even though all use sunlight.


10.2 Wind, water, and geothermal energy add to the renewable energy portfolio
Uneven solar heating contributes to pressure differences and moving air. A wind turbine extracts part of that air’s kinetic energy, turns a rotor and drives a generator. Wind speed is therefore a resource condition, not a promise of constant electrical output. Turbines have operating ranges, rated output limits and protective shutdown conditions. A turbine that has stopped in very strong wind illustrates a device constraint, not the absence of kinetic energy in the air. [Book, pp. 302–303.]


Inside a wind turbine





Reconstructed illustration adapted from Molles & Borrell, Environment: Science, Issues, Solutions (2016), Fig. 10.8. The geared turbine shown is one design; direct-drive turbines omit a gearbox. DOE: wind-turbine mechanisms.

Enlarge figure


Moving air turns the rotorAerodynamic lift and drag on shaped blades produce torque. A conventional turbine does not require a spinning Magnus cylinder.


Transmit mechanical powerThe shaft transfers rotation. In this geared example, the gearbox increases rotational speed for the generator.


Generate electricityThe generator converts mechanical work into electrical energy. The resource experiment below explores why output has operating limits.



The moving outline guides attention; it does not measure energy, fluid speed or system performance. Use the experiments for numerical comparisons.

Predict. For two imaginary 1 MW systems, predict the effect of reducing sunlight from 100% to 50%. Then predict the effect of changing wind speed from 6 to 12 m/s, and from 12 to 25 m/s. Explain whether you expect a linear relationship in each case.

Worked results: why the responses differ

In A, PV output is 1,000 kW and wind output is approximately 111.1 kW. In B, PV falls to 500 kW while wind remains unchanged. In C, wind reaches 1,000 kW. In D, wind output is zero because this fictional machine reaches its protective cut-out threshold; PV remains at 500 kW.
The PV model assumes a proportional response to light under otherwise fixed conditions. The wind model includes a nonlinear increase, a rated-output limit and a cut-out threshold. Air contains kinetic energy above the threshold, but the machine is not operating to harvest it. Actual output depends on the specific device and conditions; these values are not a real turbine specification.
Do not infer annual generation from one instant. To estimate energy, we need the output over time. A single windy afternoon does not establish a yearly capacity factor.

For the physical mechanisms, compare the Department of Energy’s explanations of photovoltaic cells and wind-turbine conversion. The DOE turbine overview also explains operating limits. The exact numerical curve above is an original teaching model.
Hydropower converts gravitational potential and kinetic energy in water into mechanical rotation and electricity. A reservoir can store water and shift some production in time, subject to inflow, ecological requirements and other uses. A run-of-river system usually has much less storage; diversion may still alter the river reach between intake and return. Tides arise from gravitational interactions, while most surface-wave energy derives from wind. “Renewable” does not imply an identical primary driver or identical controllability. [Book, pp. 304–306.]


Hydropower: a useful height difference





Reconstructed illustration adapted from Molles & Borrell, Environment: Science, Issues, Solutions (2016), Fig. 10.12. The schematic shows a reservoir-based plant; output depends on flow, hydraulic head and efficiency.

Enlarge figure


Water has gravitational potential energyA difference in water level provides hydraulic head. Both the height difference and the flow rate matter.


Flow drives a turbineWater passes through the penstock and turbine, transferring energy to the shaft.


Generate electricity, return waterThe generator converts rotation into electricity. Returning water downstream does not undo changes to flow timing, sediment or fish passage.



The moving outline guides attention; it does not measure energy, fluid speed or system performance. Use the experiments for numerical comparisons.


Geothermal systems use heat within Earth, including heat associated with radioactive decay. They do not depend on daily sunshine. In dry-steam systems, steam drives a turbine directly; in flash-steam systems, a pressure reduction causes some hot water to vaporize; in binary-cycle systems, a heat exchanger transfers heat to a separate fluid with a lower boiling point. The geothermal water and secondary fluid need not mix. A useful design depends on local temperature and geology. [Book, pp. 306–307; EIA geothermal explanation.]


Binary geothermal: heat crosses between fluids





Reconstructed illustration adapted from Molles & Borrell, Environment: Science, Issues, Solutions (2016), Fig. 10.19. This is a binary-cycle plant, not a dry-steam or flash-steam plant. Well geometry and subsurface flow are schematic.

Enlarge figure


Bring geothermal heat to the surfaceHot geothermal fluid carries energy from the reservoir to a heat exchanger.


Heat a separate working fluidHeat crosses the exchanger without requiring the two fluids to mix. The secondary fluid vaporizes and drives a turbine.


Condense and recirculateThe working fluid condenses, while cooled geothermal fluid returns through an injection well. Sustainable operation depends on the reservoir and management.



The moving outline guides attention; it does not measure energy, fluid speed or system performance. Use the experiments for numerical comparisons.


Compare: solar PV, a reservoir hydro plant and geothermal generation differ in resource availability and controllability. Avoid reducing these differences to “renewable energy is always intermittent.” Ask which source, which site and which operating constraint.



10.3 Biomass fuels represent stored chemical energy
Photosynthesis stores solar energy in biological material. Burning wood or other biomass releases chemical energy as heat. Biomass is renewable only when its production and management support renewal at the relevant rate; a growing resource can still be depleted by harvesting too quickly.
Liquid biofuels require additional conversion. Sugars can be fermented to produce ethanol. Cellulosic feedstocks first require treatment that makes sugars available for fermentation, followed by separation of the product. Biodiesel follows a different processing route from fats or oils. The energy, water, nutrients and land required for these steps belong in the assessment—not just the energy in the final fuel. [Book, pp. 307–309.]


Cellulosic ethanol: making sugars accessible





Reconstructed illustration adapted from Molles & Borrell, Environment: Science, Issues, Solutions (2016), Fig. 10.23. Process vessels and the molecular inset are conceptual; this is not a molecular-structure or engineering diagram.

Enlarge figure


Prepare plant materialPretreatment makes cellulose more accessible. The feedstock still carries land, water and harvesting impacts.


Release fermentable sugarsEnzymes break cellulose into sugars that microorganisms can use.


Ferment and recover ethanolMicroorganisms convert sugars into ethanol. Separating the fuel also requires energy and belongs in the life-cycle accounting.



The moving outline guides attention; it does not measure energy, fluid speed or system performance. Use the experiments for numerical comparisons.


Algae and nonfood feedstocks offer possibilities, but a promising laboratory pathway is not automatically a low-impact commercial system. Growing, harvesting and processing the feedstock can be demanding. Identify which limitation a proposed improvement actually addresses.

Conversion-pathway game


Offline challenge: explain the next step after sunlight reaches a PV cell, mirrors heat a fluid, geothermal water enters a binary plant, cellulose enters ethanol processing, and tidal water begins moving.




Offline answers and discussion

PV uses a semiconductor and separated charge carriers. CSP supplies a thermal power cycle. Binary geothermal transfers heat to a separate working fluid. Cellulose must be converted into accessible sugars before fermentation. Tidal motion depends directly on gravitational interactions. Compare the physical conversion in each answer, not simply its renewable label.

title: Chapter 10: Renewable Energy
text:
Issues · Renewable is not impact-free

10.4 Solar power remains costly and can damage the environment
This is the book’s official section heading. Its cost wording reflects the publication context of 2016, not a claim about today’s prices or rankings. The durable lesson is to specify what a cost or impact includes: a device, an installed project, energy delivered, integration requirements, or an entire life cycle.
Large solar installations can alter habitats and land use. Desert ecosystems are not empty simply because vegetation is sparse. Water demand depends strongly on whether the installation is PV or a thermal plant and on its cooling design. Land preparation, roads and transmission connections extend the footprint beyond the collector area. [Book, pp. 310–312.]
Energy return on energy invested (EROEI) compares energy delivered with energy used to obtain it. The denominator is invested energy—not money and not incoming sunlight. State a common boundary before comparing two values: do both include manufacturing, construction, operation, replacement and decommissioning? The book’s marginal definition supports the returned/invested ratio used here; an inverted sentence in the running text should not reverse it.

Net-energy experiment
Keep delivered energy at 100 units and increase the investment. Predict both the ratio and the net amount before moving the slider.


Without JavaScript: EROEI = delivered energy ÷ invested energy; net energy = delivered − invested. For delivery of 100 and investment of 10, the ratio is 10 and net energy is 90 units.




Worked trials and limits

For delivery of 100 units, investments of 10, 25, 100 and 125 give EROEI values of 10, 4, 1 and 0.8, respectively. Corresponding net energy is 90, 75, 0 and −25 units. At a ratio of one, this boundary leaves no net energy. These invented examples are not ratings for specific technologies. An attractive ratio does not by itself establish acceptable wildlife effects, affordability or supply at the right time.




10.5 Wind turbines and transmission lines kill birds and bats
Wildlife effects can involve collisions and changes in habitat use. Species, migration routes, season, weather, rotor operation and transmission layout influence exposure. A national total does not establish the effect on a particular local population, and a count without search effort or detection information can be misleading. [Book, pp. 312–314.]
Separate hazard, exposure and population consequence. A moving rotor presents a hazard; animals’ use of the site influences exposure; mortality relative to population size and reproductive capacity affects the biological consequence. This chain suggests measurements and interventions more precisely than saying that wind is either harmless or unacceptable.
Design a study: compare operation under a curtailment rule with a suitable comparison condition. Measure fatalities with appropriate detection corrections, energy generated, and relevant weather or seasonal conditions. An intervention should be evaluated on both its ecological result and its energy tradeoff.


10.6 Hydroelectric development can have multiple environmental and social impacts
Hydroelectric projects can alter flow timing, sediment transport, water temperature, oxygen conditions and fish movement. A reservoir transforms a flowing-river habitat and can inundate land. Effects propagate upstream and downstream, so the project boundary cannot stop at the dam wall.
The chapter’s Three Gorges and Belo Monte examples connect electricity benefits to displaced communities and changed livelihoods. Treat these as historical case studies, not current project-status reports. Ask who participates in decisions, how alternatives are compared and whether compensation addresses the actual losses. A benefit to distant electricity users does not cancel a local burden by definition. [Book, pp. 314–315.]


The human side of a reservoir





Molles & Borrell, Environment: Science, Issues, Solutions (2016), Fig. 10.34, reproduced from the supplied Chapter 10 presentation. A resident in a partly demolished home before inundation by the Three Gorges reservoir. Displacement can involve losing a home, income, access to land and community ties; a photograph alone cannot establish every outcome.

Enlarge figure

Reservoir greenhouse-gas effects vary with site and conditions. “No fossil fuel burned at the turbine” is not equivalent to “no life-cycle emissions.” The same boundary discipline used in Chapter 9 applies here.


10.7 Biofuel development can reduce food supplies and harm the environment
Land allocated to a fuel crop may compete with food production or other uses. Expansion can cause direct or indirect land-use change; fertilization, water use and pesticide application add further pathways. A fuel crop that regrows does not automatically reverse the loss of a diverse ecosystem or its stored carbon.
The chapter discusses food–fuel tensions as one contributor within larger food systems. Do not attribute every food-price change to biofuels alone: harvests, demand, markets and other conditions also matter. A causal argument needs more than two trends moving together. [Book, pp. 315–317.]
Counterfactual question: what would happen to the land or residue without fuel production? A material called “waste” may already protect soil, return nutrients or support another use. Full accounting compares the new pathway with that alternative, not with an imaginary world in which the material has no function.

title: Chapter 10: Renewable Energy
section: Solutions · Match the intervention to the impact
text:
Solutions · Match the intervention to the impact

10.8 Smart solutions to issues associated with solar power are under development
Different solutions address different constraints. Rooftops, parking areas and previously disturbed sites may reduce new habitat conversion. Dry or hybrid cooling can reduce water use in appropriate thermal systems, with design and performance tradeoffs. Better connections and project processes can address deployment barriers, but policy examples in the book are historical rather than current incentive advice. [Book, pp. 317–319.]


A siting alternative on existing buildings





Molles & Borrell, Environment: Science, Issues, Solutions (2016), Fig. 10.40, reproduced from the supplied presentation. Rooftop PV in Freiburg, Germany. Suitable existing roofs can reduce pressure to clear intact habitat; structural suitability, shading and grid connections still need assessment.

Enlarge figure

Thermal storage stores heat for later conversion; batteries store energy in another form. Neither creates additional primary energy. Storage changes timing and incurs losses or other constraints. Pairing generation with flexible demand can also improve timing: operating a suitable load during abundant supply is not the same as reducing its total energy use.
Choose a match: if the problem is desert habitat loss, an evaluation of disturbed-land alternatives addresses the mechanism more directly than a larger battery. If the problem is evening demand after sunset, the timing of supply and demand becomes central.


10.9 Less damaging wind-generation strategies are under development
Siting can avoid sensitive habitats and movement corridors. Operation can be adjusted during periods of elevated wildlife exposure. The chapter describes studies using higher starting wind speeds and other selective curtailment strategies to reduce bat mortality. These are empirical, site-specific comparisons, not a universal guarantee or a single permanent percentage for every wind farm. [Book, pp. 319–321.]
Repowering, transmission routing and line treatments can address additional issues. A disturbed site still needs ecological assessment; “already altered” does not mean “no species use it.” A strong plan states the operating rule, monitoring method, acceptable response threshold and who will revise the rule when evidence changes.


10.10 Downsizing can mitigate the impacts of hydroelectric development
Smaller or run-of-river projects can avoid some large-reservoir impacts. Retrofitting suitable existing structures may avoid building a new barrier. But size alone is not an impact assessment: a diversion can reduce flow in a bypassed reach, and many small projects can produce cumulative effects. [Book, pp. 321–323.]
Protecting ecological flows, sediment movement and fish passage requires attention to the actual river and species. A device advertised as fish-friendly still needs evidence under relevant conditions. Ask how operation changes across seasons and droughts, not just how it performs at one flow rate.
River negotiation: assign teams to electricity supply, aquatic ecology and downstream water users. Agree on the information needed to set a minimum-flow rule. Explain what would happen when water is insufficient to meet all desired uses. The exercise is about explicit priorities and evidence—not inventing a universally safe percentage.


10.11 Less damaging, more efficient biofuels are under development as alternatives to oil-based fuels
Cellulosic materials, perennial crops, residues and selected wastes may reduce some competition with food crops or some land-use burdens. The advantage depends on the feedstock, location, processing and alternative use. Residue removal must account for soil protection and nutrients; perennial production still needs a land-use comparison. [Book, pp. 323–325.]
Algae can incorporate carbon dioxide during growth, but burning the resulting fuel returns carbon to the atmosphere. Temporary uptake is not permanent sequestration. Energy used in cultivation, harvesting, drying and conversion affects the net result. A more efficient process should be demonstrated with a consistent energy and material balance.
The solution is therefore not to attach a “sustainable” label to a feedstock category. Screen the full pathway, protect high-value ecosystems, improve processing, monitor effects and revise the choice if the promised advantage fails to appear.

Environmental-safeguards challenge


Offline challenge: match habitat-sensitive solar siting, targeted wind curtailment, ecological river flows and careful feedstock selection to their respective impact pathways.




Offline answers and extension

For solar habitat loss, evaluate rooftops and disturbed land. For the stated low-wind bat-exposure problem, test targeted curtailment and monitor it. For a dewatered river reach, protect ecological flow and fish passage. For biofuel-driven habitat conversion, screen feedstocks and land use while accounting for soil needs. Add one measurable indicator to each answer; no safeguard is established merely by naming it.

title: Chapter 10: Renewable Energy
text:
Chapter takeaways

Name the conversion: PV, solar heat, wind, water, geothermal and biomass do not work in the same way.
Keep the denominators straight: efficiency, EROEI and capacity factor answer different questions.
Distinguish totals from timing: enough energy over a day does not guarantee supply in each period.
Match solutions to impacts: siting, curtailment, ecological flows and feedstock choices act on different mechanisms.
Evaluate the whole system: include land, water, wildlife, communities, life-cycle boundaries and monitoring—not only electrical output.

Answer the central question: renewable resources can support energy services while reducing some burdens of fossil systems, but no project is automatically free of environmental effects. A defensible transition combines efficient services, appropriate technology and siting, participation, ecological safeguards and evidence-based revision. “Lower impact under these conditions” is a stronger scientific claim than “impact-free.”

title: Chapter 10: Renewable Energy
text:
Science: different resources, different conversions

Renewable and low carbon describe different properties
A renewable resource replenishes on timescales relevant to use. Biomass additionally requires management consistent with renewal. Low carbon describes emissions under a specified boundary. Neither term means that a project has no land, water or community impacts. Nuclear illustrates the distinction: low operational combustion emissions do not make uranium renewable. [Textbook, p. 297; connection to Chapter 9.]


A resource is not yet a service
Use the same chain for each technology: resource → conversion device → energy carrier → useful service. For a solar-powered refrigerator, sunlight reaches a photovoltaic device, electrical energy travels through a circuit, and the refrigerator transfers heat out of its interior. The service is food preservation—not “using electricity” for its own sake.
This distinction opens two kinds of solution. You can change the energy supply, or provide the same service with less demand. A well-insulated refrigerator and a different electricity source act at different places in the chain; they are not competing definitions of renewable energy.


Solar energy
Photovoltaic cells convert light into electricity in a semiconductor. Light energizes charge carriers, and an internal electric field helps separate them. A connected circuit carries current. No steam turbine is required in this conversion.
Concentrating solar power (CSP) uses mirrors to collect sunlight as heat. The heat supports a power cycle and can, in suitable designs, be stored for later use. Solar heating supplies heat directly for a service such as hot water. Water requirements depend on the technology and its cooling system. [Textbook, pp. 301, 311, 325; US Department of Energy.]


Wind and water
Wind results largely from uneven solar heating and associated pressure differences. A rotor captures part of the moving air’s kinetic energy, and a generator converts rotation to electricity. Output depends on conditions and operational limits.
Hydroelectric systems use water moving under gravity. A reservoir can shift some generation in time, subject to water availability and operating constraints. Run-of-river systems generally have little storage. Tidal motion has gravitational origins; most wave energy originates with wind. Predictability, variability and controllability are distinct properties. [Textbook, pp. 303–305, 321.]


Geothermal energy
Geothermal systems draw on internal Earth heat, including heat associated with radioactive decay and heat remaining from Earth’s formation. Temperature and local geology influence whether heat can supply electricity or a direct heating service. This differs from a ground-source heat pump, which uses electricity to transfer heat.
The book’s short summary simplifies Earth’s heat source. The EIA explanation provides useful clarification. The chapter’s dry-steam, flash-steam and binary-cycle examples demonstrate that conversion design depends on resource conditions. [Textbook, p. 307.]


Biomass and biofuels
Wood, residues and other biological materials store chemical energy. Ethanol can come from sugars or from cellulose broken into fermentable sugars. Biodiesel can come from fats or oils. Growing algae and converting cellulosic material introduce additional processing challenges.
Combustion releases carbon. Whether regrowth offsets that release depends on land use, management, time and what would have happened without the harvest. Food competition, nutrient removal, water demands and habitat conversion belong in the assessment. Residues can avoid some impacts of dedicated crops, but removing residues also affects soils. [Textbook, pp. 307, 309, 315, 323, 325.]

title: Chapter 10: Renewable Energy
text:
Three quantities worth keeping separate








Quantity
Calculation
What it answers




Conversion efficiency
Useful energy out / energy input
How much of an input becomes the desired output?


Energy return on energy invested (EROEI)
Energy delivered / energy invested in obtaining it
How much energy does the system return for the energy spent?


Capacity factor
Actual energy / (rated power × elapsed time)
How much did a plant produce relative to continuous rated output?



EROEI is not a financial return and does not capture every environmental effect. Compare studies only when their boundaries and energy accounting are compatible. [Textbook, p. 311.]
Example 1, invented for practice: a system delivers 100 energy units and requires 10 units to obtain them. Its EROEI is 10 and its net energy is 90 units.
Example 2, invented for practice: a 10 MW plant with a 25% capacity factor over 24 hours generates \(10\times24\times0.25=60\) MWh. That total does not tell us when the energy arrives.


Check: if the investment rises to 25 units, what changes?

With delivery still at 100 units, EROEI falls to 4 and net energy falls to 75 units. This alone says nothing about wildlife effects, affordability or whether generation coincides with demand.


The denominator tells you the question
An efficiency of 25% and a capacity factor of 25% are not interchangeable. Efficiency compares output energy with input energy. Capacity factor compares actual output with the output possible at continuous rated power over the same interval. EROEI compares delivered energy with energy invested in obtaining it, according to a defined accounting boundary.
Retrieval check: say each denominator aloud without looking at the table. Then explain why a 1 MW nameplate rating is not a promise of 24 MWh every day. Availability of the resource and operational conditions affect the time-integrated output.

Model assumptions: periods are eight hours each; solar output factors are 0, 1 and 0; wind factors are 1, 0.5 and 1, multiplied by 0.25 during weak wind. Efficiency reduces all demand first, then load shifting moves equal MW from evening to midday. Storage starts empty, charges only from renewable surplus, and returns 80% of charged energy. “Charging allowance” is a simplified input-energy capacity, not a commercial battery nameplate rating. The discharge control limits returned power; a separate charging-power constraint is omitted. Remaining deficits require additional supply. Leftover stored energy and curtailed surplus do not serve another day in this model.
Limits: this is an energy-balance exercise, not a reliability or cost study. It omits hourly fluctuations, seasonal weather, outages, network congestion, reserves, degradation, construction and operating costs. Passing the three periods cannot certify a real grid.

Experiment 10.2: diagnose, do not just add capacity
Run these controlled trials before trying to find a successful portfolio. Reset the baseline between trials so only one variable changes.

Follow the baseline day. At the end of midday, the battery has accepted 400 MWh. The display shows 320 MWh of remaining deliverable energy because the model assigns 20% round-trip losses. At the end of evening, that stored energy has been used and 80 MWh still needs another supply.
Double the charging allowance to 800 MWh. Predict whether it helps. There is still only 400 MWh of surplus to charge it. Extra empty capacity cannot create energy.
Reset and reduce the discharge limit to 20 MW. The battery can return at most \(20\times8=160\) MWh in the evening. Inspect both the unmet demand and the energy still in the store. Why can a charged battery fail to serve a load?
Reset and reduce the charging allowance to 200 MWh. Compare this result with trial 3. Do equal shortfalls necessarily imply the same cause?



Interpret the two 240 MWh shortfalls

With a 20 MW discharge limit, only 160 MWh can leave the store during the eight-hour evening. The 400 MWh evening gap therefore leaves 240 MWh for other supply. Another 160 MWh remains deliverable in storage; the limiting factor is power over this interval.
With a 200 MWh charging allowance and the original 40 MW discharge limit, only 160 MWh is deliverable after losses. The same 240 MWh shortage remains, but the battery is now depleted. The limiting factor is stored energy. One result, two mechanisms: diagnose before choosing an intervention.
Increasing storage to 800 MWh in trial 2 leaves the baseline 80 MWh shortfall unchanged. The store has insufficient surplus energy to charge beyond 400 MWh. Inspecting a daily total alone would miss these distinctions.

title: Chapter 10: Renewable Energy
text:
Classroom activity: redesign Riverton
Work in the same teams as Chapter 9, or write an individual recommendation at your own pace. The numerical exercise is an original extension of the book’s environmental comparisons.

Reproduce the baseline and explain the 80 MWh shortfall.
Find a normal-day plan with no additional modeled supply.
Record all six controls and one environmental burden your plan creates.
After three minutes of design, switch to weak wind. Quantify the new deficit and revise your plan.
Give a recommendation that includes a safeguard and a limitation of the model.



Worked normal-day solution

Keep solar at 100 MW, wind at 40 MW, storage allowance at 400 MWh and discharge limit at 40 MW. Reduce demand by 10% and shift 10 MW from evening into midday.
Demand becomes 36, 73 and 71 MW. Renewable generation remains 40, 120 and 40 MW. Surplus charging is 32 MWh in the first period and 376 MWh at midday, but the 400 MWh storage limit curtails 8 MWh. Evening requires 248 MWh, within both the stored-energy and discharge-power limits. No modeled backup is required.
There are many possible solutions. The model assigns no costs, so it cannot identify the cheapest one.



Weak-wind result and one revised solution

For the normal-day solution above, weak wind reduces renewable generation to 10, 105 and 10 MW. The first period needs 26 MW of additional supply. Midday stores 256 MWh, returning at most 204.8 MWh in the evening. Evening backup is 35.4 MW. Total additional energy is 491.2 MWh.
One feasible stressed-day combination is solar 180 MW, wind 130 MW, storage allowance 500 MWh, discharge limit 60 MW, efficiency 20% and load shift 10 MW. Demand becomes 32, 66 and 62 MW, while weak-wind renewable output is 32.5, 196.25 and 32.5 MW. Storage receives 4 MWh early and reaches its 500 MWh limit at midday. Evening requires 236 MWh, below the 400 MWh deliverable-energy limit and the power limit. All modeled periods meet demand.
As a diagnostic check, reducing wind to 120 MW leaves a 2 MW shortfall in the first period even though later periods can be served. A valid solution must check every period.
The extra capacity creates real questions about cost, land, transmission and ecological effects. Passing this simplified stress case does not establish seasonal adequacy.



Instructor facilitation and scoring

Use the preceding experiment to introduce the model, then allow time to design, stress-test, revise and evaluate ecological consequences. Extend the investigation as needed. If devices are unavailable, use the baseline table and a calculator. The companion presentation has its own 50-minute timing.
Rubric, 8 points: correct energy/power calculation (2), a recorded and reproducible balance (2), ecological burden and relevant safeguard (2), a defensible stress response and limitation (2). A team can earn credit for correctly diagnosing an infeasible plan.
Ask: “Which control changes generation, which changes timing, and which reduces the service’s energy requirement?” The distinctions matter more than finding one favored portfolio.

title: Chapter 10: Renewable Energy
section: Issues and solutions beyond the electricity balance
text:
Issues and solutions beyond the electricity balance

Solar and wind siting
Solar development can affect habitats and water demand, depending on the technology. Roofs or already disturbed sites can reduce some new land conversion. Wind siting and operation affect birds and bats. Selective curtailment can reduce exposure during periods of elevated risk, but performance should be assessed locally. Transmission infrastructure belongs in the same evaluation. [Textbook, pp. 311, 313, 319–321.]


Rivers and communities
Hydropower can change flow, sediment movement, water quality and fish passage. Flooding can displace communities. The textbook’s Three Gorges and Belo Monte discussions illustrate differences between those receiving electricity and those bearing local impacts. Treat them as historical case studies, not current project-status reports.
Smaller or run-of-river projects can reduce some effects, but diversion and cumulative impacts still need assessment. A low-carbon objective does not remove the need for meaningful participation by affected communities. [Textbook, pp. 315, 321, 323.]


Biofuel choices
Feedstock choice connects fuel to food systems and land use. Cellulosic materials, residues or algae may avoid some impacts associated with food crops, but processing energy, nutrients, water and soil functions still matter. Evaluate a complete pathway before calling it sustainable. [Textbook, pp. 309, 315, 323–325.]


A transition needs a sequence
A target portfolio needs interconnection, construction, procurement and participation. Efficiency can reduce needs while other projects develop. Monitoring must connect indicators to decisions: an observed ecological effect should trigger a specified response. State who will monitor, what they will measure and when the plan will be reviewed.


Turn a numerical solution into a scientific recommendation
Choose one intervention in your grid design and complete this chain: decision → potential burden → safeguard → monitoring indicator → response. For example, new wind generation prompts questions about site-specific wildlife exposure; siting and selective curtailment may be safeguards, but their effectiveness must be measured and reviewed. The energy simulator does not supply those ecological measurements.
A strong conclusion can therefore say: “Our recorded settings meet the modeled periods under this wind scenario. Before recommending construction, we would need ; we would monitor  and revise the plan if ___.” This is stronger than claiming the simulation has proved the whole system sustainable.

title: Chapter 10: Renewable Energy
text:
Review and exit ticket


Why can daily supply equal daily demand while the system fails?

Energy may arrive in the wrong period. Surplus does not automatically serve a later deficit. Storage, flexible loads, other supply and network connections can help, subject to their constraints.



Why does doubling battery capacity not always fix a shortfall?

The battery needs energy to charge, sufficient charging and discharge power, and enough capacity. Losses reduce returned energy. An empty, larger battery cannot create electricity.



What would make a renewable recommendation environmentally defensible?

A clear comparison boundary, quantified service requirements, an identified ecological burden, participation by affected communities, and a safeguard with a monitoring plan.

Final reflection: explain the timing problem, identify a battery limitation, and propose one ecological safeguard. Return to the chapter’s central question and distinguish reduced impacts from an absence of impacts.

title: Chapter 1: Mathematical Foundations
text:
1.1 Fractions, percentages, and exponents

Fractions and proportions
A fraction represents a part relative to a whole. A proportion states that two ratios are equal.
\[
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}
\]
Cross-multiplication gives \(ad=bc\), which lets us solve for an unknown quantity.

Statistical example
In a sample of 80 observations, 28 belong to category A. The sample proportion is
\[
\hat p=\frac{28}{80}=0.35.
\]
This can be reported as a decimal, \(0.35\), or a percentage, \(35\%\).



Percentages and percentage change
To convert a proportion to a percentage, multiply by 100. Percentage change compares the change to the original value:
\[
\text{Percentage change}=\frac{\text{new}-\text{original}}{\text{original}}\times100\%.
\]
If a group mean increases from 40 to 46, the absolute increase is 6 and the percentage increase is
\[
\frac{46-40}{40}\times100\%=15\%.
\]
An increase of 6 points and an increase of 15% describe the same change using different scales.


Exponents and roots
Exponents describe repeated multiplication. Roots reverse exponentiation.

\(a^m a^n=a^{m+n}\)    ·    \(\frac{a^m}{a^n}=a^{m-n}\)    ·    \((a^m)^n=a^{mn}\)    ·    \(a^{-n}=\frac{1}{a^n}\)

Square roots appear throughout statistics. For example, the standard error of a mean is
\[
SE_{\bar x}=\frac{s}{\sqrt n}.
\]
When \(s=12\) and \(n=36\), \(SE=12/6=2\).


Check 1.1: A sample contains 45 successes among 120 observations. What percentage are successes?


\(\hat p=45/120=0.375\). Multiplying by 100 gives 37.5%.

title: Chapter 1: Mathematical Foundations
text:
1.2 Basic algebra

Order of operations
Evaluate expressions in this order: grouping symbols, exponents, multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction.
For \(3+2(5-1)^2\):
\[
3+2(4)^2=3+2(16)=35.
\]


Solving equations
An equation stays balanced when the same valid operation is applied to both sides.

Solve for an unknown mean
Suppose the standardized score is \(z=1.5\), the raw score is \(x=86\), and the standard deviation is \(s=8\):
\[
z=\frac{x-\bar x}{s}.
\]
Substitute and solve:
\[
1.5=\frac{86-\bar x}{8}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
12=86-\bar x
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\bar x=74.
\]



Summation notation
The symbol \(\sum\) tells us to add a sequence of values. For observations \(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n\),
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i=x_1+x_2+\cdots+x_n.
\]
The sample mean is
\[
\bar x=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i.
\]
For scores \(4,7,8,11\), the mean is \((4+7+8+11)/4=7.5\).


Check 1.2: Rearrange \(SE=s/\sqrt n\) to solve for \(n\).


Multiply by \(\sqrt n\), divide by \(SE\), and square both sides:
\[
\sqrt n=\frac{s}{SE}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
n=\left(\frac{s}{SE}\right)^2.
\]

title: Chapter 1: Mathematical Foundations
text:
1.3 Functions and graphs
A function maps each permitted input to exactly one output. We write \(y=f(x)\).

Linear functions
The equation
\[
y=\beta_0+\beta_1x
\]
describes a straight line. The intercept \(\beta_0\) is the expected value of \(y\) when \(x=0\). The slope \(\beta_1\) is the expected change in \(y\) for a one-unit increase in \(x\).

Interpreting a model
For \(\widehat{Score}=62+3.5(Hours)\):

The predicted score at zero study hours is 62.
Each additional study hour is associated with a 3.5-point increase in the predicted score.
At 4 hours, the predicted score is \(62+3.5(4)=76\).




Reading a graph
Before interpreting a graph, ask:

What quantities are on the axes?
What are their units and scales?
Does the graph show individual observations, summaries, or model predictions?
Is the relationship increasing, decreasing, curved, clustered, or interrupted by outliers?
Does the graph support description, prediction, or a causal conclusion?



Check 1.3: In \(\hat y=18-0.7x\), what does the slope mean?


For every one-unit increase in \(x\), the predicted value of \(y\) decreases by 0.7 units. The negative sign indicates the direction.

title: Chapter 1: Mathematical Foundations
text:
1.4 Introduction to probability
Probability quantifies uncertainty on a scale from 0 to 1.
\[
0\leq P(A)\leq1.
\]
The sample space contains every possible outcome. An event is a collection of outcomes within that sample space.

1.4.1 Coin flips
For one fair coin flip, \(S=\{H,T\}\), and
\[
P(H)=P(T)=\frac12.
\]
For two independent fair flips, \(S=\{HH,HT,TH,TT\}\). The probability of exactly one head is
\[
P(HT\text{ or }TH)=\frac24=\frac12.
\]


1.4.2 Simple events
The complement \(A^c\) contains outcomes where \(A\) does not occur:
\[
P(A^c)=1-P(A).
\]
For mutually exclusive events \(A\) and \(B\):
\[
P(A\text{ or }B)=P(A)+P(B).
\]
For independent events:
\[
P(A\text{ and }B)=P(A)P(B).
\]

Use the complement
If the probability that an instrument fails on a given trial is \(0.03\), the probability it does not fail is
\[
1-0.03=0.97.
\]



Check 1.4: What is the probability of at least one head in two fair coin flips?


Use the complement. The only outcome with no heads is \(TT\), which has probability \(1/4\):
\[
P(\text{at least one head})=1-P(TT)=1-\frac14=\frac34.
\]

Renewable energy also has impacts: solar land and water use, wind-related wildlife mortality, river disruption, and biofuel competition with food and habitats.
Use rooftop solar and water-saving designs, wildlife-sensitive wind operation, lower-impact hydropower, and biofuels from wastes or other lower-impact feedstocks.
Compare renewable energy sources and energy returns; evaluate why renewable does not automatically mean environmentally sustainable.
295


11Environmental Health, Risk, and Toxicology
What is the relationship between the environment and human health and how can we manage that relationship?
Persistent toxins, bioaccumulation, biomagnification, endocrine disruption, emerging diseases, and antibiotic or pesticide resistance threaten health.
Assess hazards, dose–response relationships, and exposure; apply precaution; coordinate public-health measures and use evolutionary principles to manage resistance.
Distinguish hazard from risk and bioaccumulation from biomagnification; explain risk assessment and how resistance evolves.
329


12Solid and Hazardous Waste Management
How can we reduce the environmental impact of solid waste and dispose of hazardous waste safely?
Growing waste streams, unsafe disposal, electronic waste, international waste shipments, and long-lived radioactive waste pose contamination and storage challenges.
Prioritize waste reduction, recycling, and composting; track and treat hazardous wastes; use engineered disposal and international controls on hazardous-waste trade.
Distinguish solid and hazardous waste; compare prevention, recovery, treatment, and disposal, including the challenges of long-term containment.
357


13Air, Water, and Soil Pollution
How can we control and reduce environmental pollution?
Air pollution, acid deposition, persistent contaminants, and excess organic matter or nutrients harm health, food webs, and ecosystem functioning.
Combine regulation and emissions controls with cleaner indoor technologies, contaminated-site remediation, wastewater treatment, and constructed wetlands.
Trace pollutant sources and transport; explain acid deposition, food-chain contamination, and eutrophication; match pollution problems to appropriate controls.
385

How can we mitigate and adapt to the environmental and social impacts of climate change?
Fossil-fuel emissions raise atmospheric carbon dioxide; warming changes Earth systems and creates ecological, economic, and societal risks.
Reduce emissions through energy and transport changes and economic policies; protect carbon sinks, assess carbon capture, and plan for adaptation.
Explain the greenhouse effect, carbon-cycle changes, and feedbacks; evaluate evidence of human influence and distinguish mitigation from adaptation.

title: Chapter 9: Fossil Fuels and Nuclear Energy
text:
Science · Understand the energy pathways

9.1 Fossil fuels provide energy in chemical form
Fossil fuels are concentrated stores of chemical energy derived largely from ancient organisms. Those organisms captured solar energy through photosynthesis; burial and geological transformation produced materials we extract today. Formation is far slower than present-day consumption, so these fuels are nonrenewable on human timescales.
Coal develops from accumulated plant material, often associated with ancient wetlands. Burial, heat and pressure change its composition. Lignite, subbituminous coal, bituminous coal and anthracite differ in carbon content, moisture and other properties. A higher rank is not a complete environmental score: sulfur content, extraction method and power-plant controls matter too. The book’s energy-content diagram should not be read as an indefinitely increasing relationship with rank.
Petroleum develops from organic material buried in sediments, commonly originating in aquatic organisms. Geological heat transforms the material; fluids can migrate and accumulate where porous rock and an overlying seal provide a trap. Crude oil is a mixture, not a single substance. Refining separates fractions with different boiling ranges, supplying fuels as well as lubricants and chemical feedstocks. A refinery is therefore not simply an electricity-generating plant.
Natural gas consists predominantly of methane. It can occur with oil, in coal formations, or within low-permeability rock. A large resource underground is not identical to a reserve that can be extracted under specified technical and economic conditions. Reported reserves depend on those conditions and on the date of assessment. The book’s reserve maps are historical snapshots, not current inventories. [Book, pp. 264–269.]


Inside a fractionating column





Reconstructed teaching illustration adapted from Molles & Borrell, Environment: Science, Issues, Solutions (2016), Fig. 9.5, printed p. 267. Products separate across boiling ranges; the arrangement is schematic.

Enlarge figure


Heat the mixtureCrude oil contains many hydrocarbons. Heating vaporizes much of the mixture before it enters the column.


A temperature gradientThe lower column is hotter and the upper column cooler. Vapors rise and components condense over different temperature ranges.


Collect useful fractionsLighter fractions leave higher in the column; heavier fractions leave lower down. Refining separates a mixture rather than creating energy.



The moving outline guides attention; it does not measure energy, fluid speed or system performance. Use the experiments for numerical comparisons.




Gas, oil and coal in a geological setting





Reconstructed conceptual cross-section from the Chapter 9 presentation, accompanying Molles & Borrell, Environment: Science, Issues, Solutions (2016), §9.1, pp. 268–269. Oil lies below gas within the illustrated trap, and the coal seam lies higher than this oil reservoir. This is one geological arrangement, not a universal vertical sequence.

Enlarge figure


Fuel-pathway challenge


Match each clue to coal, crude oil, natural gas or uranium: buried wetland plants; refinery fractions; a methane-rich gas; controlled fission. The interactive challenge provides feedback when JavaScript is available.




Offline answer key and a deeper question

The matches are coal, crude oil, natural gas and uranium, respectively. The first three release chemical energy through combustion; uranium releases nuclear energy through fission. Explain why “all four are mined or extracted” does not mean they have the same energy-conversion mechanism.




9.2 Power plants and vehicles burn fossil fuels to generate electricity and movement
Combustion transfers chemical energy into thermal energy. In a steam-cycle plant, heat produces steam, steam rotates a turbine, and a generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy. A condenser and cooling system reject heat so the working fluid can circulate. The generator does not create energy; it changes its form.


What the generator actually does





Reconstructed teaching illustration from the Chapter 9 presentation. A simplified rotating-coil generator illustrates electromagnetic induction. See EIA: how electricity is generated. Real generator designs vary.

Enlarge figure


Supply mechanical workA turbine or another engine supplies torque to rotate the coil. The generator needs an energy input.


Change magnetic fluxAs the coil turns relative to the magnetic field, the magnetic flux through it changes, inducing a voltage.


Connect an electrical loadSlip rings and brushes connect this rotating coil to a circuit. With a load connected, mechanical work transfers energy electrically.



The moving outline guides attention; it does not measure energy, fluid speed or system performance. Use the experiments for numerical comparisons.




Fossil-fuel electricity: follow the cycle





Reconstructed teaching illustration from the Chapter 9 presentation, based on Molles & Borrell, Environment: Science, Issues, Solutions (2016), §9.2, pp. 270–272. A coal-fired steam cycle is shown; gas turbines and combined-cycle plants have different arrangements. The cooling-tower plume is condensed water droplets, distinct from combustion exhaust at the stack.

Enlarge figure


Combustion supplies heatBurning coal transfers chemical energy to the boiler. Combustion exhaust and its pollutants leave through a separate gas pathway.


Steam drives a turbineSteam expands through the turbine and turns its shaft. Thermal energy becomes mechanical work.


Rotation drives a generatorThe generator converts mechanical work into electrical energy. The cooling tower does not generate electricity.


Reject heat and return waterSteam condenses and the working water returns to the boiler. A separate cooling circuit removes rejected heat. Not all fuel energy becomes electricity.



The moving outline guides attention; it does not measure energy, fluid speed or system performance. Use the experiments for numerical comparisons.


The book illustrates a plant delivering approximately 35 units of electricity for every 100 fuel-energy units, with 65 units leaving as heat. This is a teaching example, not a rating for every plant. A combined-cycle system first uses a gas turbine, then uses its hot exhaust to supply a steam cycle. Recovering energy that would otherwise leave in the exhaust can improve overall efficiency; the book discusses efficiencies around 60% for such systems. These figures depend on design and accounting conventions. [Book, pp. 270–272.]
Vehicles connect the same idea to a different service: hot expanding gases in an internal-combustion engine produce motion, with considerable rejected heat. “Electricity generated” and “transportation supplied” are different outputs. Fair comparisons specify the service first—for example, one passenger-kilometer rather than one unit of fuel.

Experiment 9.1: follow the energy
Question: Does higher efficiency create more energy, or change where the same input goes?
Predict. With 100 input units, increase efficiency from 35% to 50%. Write down both expected outputs before moving the control. Then predict what happens if you double the input without changing efficiency.


The interactive energy-flow diagram loads when JavaScript is available. Without it, use input × efficiency for electricity and input minus electricity for rejected heat; record the trials below.


Investigate. Press Play animation to follow the pathways. The arrows show direction; the numbers—not animation speed—give the energy quantities.

Run 100 input units at 35%, then at 50%. Hold the input constant.
Run 200 input units at 50%. Hold efficiency constant.
Switch the source from coal to nuclear while keeping both numbers unchanged. What stays the same? What environmental mechanism changes?

Interpret the experiment and check your results

A produces 35 electrical units and 65 heat units; B produces 50 and 50; C produces 100 and 100. In every trial, outputs sum to input. Raising efficiency redistributes a fixed input toward useful electricity. Doubling input at fixed efficiency doubles both outputs.
Switching the heat source does not change the arithmetic because you held efficiency fixed. It changes the process supplying heat: fossil combustion releases chemical energy and combustion CO₂; fission releases nuclear energy without burning carbon. Extraction, cooling and waste must still be assessed. The model deliberately does not assign a technology-specific efficiency or emissions ranking.




9.3 Nuclear energy is released by atomic fission and fusion
Fission splits a heavy nucleus and can release neutrons that sustain further fissions. Fusion combines light nuclei. Neither is the burning of a carbon-containing fuel. The nuclear power cycle discussed here uses controlled fission as a source of heat, followed by heat transfer, a turbine and a generator. Sharing a steam cycle does not make the upstream processes or waste streams identical.
In a water-moderated reactor, the moderator slows neutrons, control rods absorb neutrons, and the coolant transfers heat. Containment provides a protective barrier. One material can perform more than one function, but the functions remain distinct. In the book’s pressurized-water example, heat crosses between separate fluid circuits; radioactive primary coolant is not simply sent through the cooling tower. [Book, pp. 272–274.]


Nuclear electricity: separate the fluid circuits





Reconstructed teaching illustration from the Chapter 9 presentation, based on Molles & Borrell, Environment: Science, Issues, Solutions (2016), §9.3, pp. 272–274. This pressurized-water example separates the primary coolant, steam cycle and cooling-water circuit. It is not a piping or safety-design specification.

Enlarge figure


Fission supplies heatControlled fission heats the fuel and primary coolant. Control rods absorb neutrons; cooling removes heat.


Transfer heat across a boundaryThe steam generator transfers heat into a separate water circuit. Radioactive primary coolant is not sent through the cooling tower.


Steam drives electricity generationThe turbine and generator use the same broad conversion sequence as other steam-cycle plants, although the source of heat differs.


Keep removing heatCondensation completes the steam cycle. Cooling also remains necessary after shutdown because radioactive products continue to release decay heat.



The moving outline guides attention; it does not measure energy, fluid speed or system performance. Use the experiments for numerical comparisons.



Reactor-control experiment
Predict what changes when rods are inserted. Then separately change cooling availability. Which control affects the chain reaction, and which affects heat removal?


Offline model: begin with 24 symbolic neutron units. A balanced generation leaves 24; an invented multiplication factor of 1.35 gives 32.4; a suppression factor of 0.2 gives 4.8. These are teaching numbers, not reactor operating parameters. Inserting rods suppresses the chain reaction but does not eliminate decay heat.


Interpretation: the animation separates two concepts, not two independent real engineering systems. Neutron absorption can stop the sustained chain reaction, while previously produced radioactive material continues releasing heat. Cooling is still needed. The model supplies no temperature, radiation dose or safety prediction. This distinction is clarified by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission’s explanation of decay heat.
Pause and explain: “The reactor is shut down, so there is no more heat.” Identify the error without using the word dangerous. A causal explanation is more informative than a label.

title: Chapter 9: Fossil Fuels and Nuclear Energy
text:
Issues · Follow the burdens

9.4 Global energy use grows as energy shortages loom
The chapter connects population, economic activity and energy services to demand. Total use and use per person answer different questions. A populous region may use more energy overall while using less per person. Figure 9.20 reports 2014 energy use of 7.22 metric tons of oil equivalent per person for the United States, 3.22 for the European Union and 2.28 for China. These are historical values with a common unit, not current comparisons. [Book, pp. 274–277, especially p. 276.]
Practice: a region with 10 million people using 2 energy units each consumes 20 million units; a region with 2 million people using 5 each consumes 10 million. Which has greater total use? Which has greater use per person? The answers differ because the denominator differs.
The phrase peak production describes a maximum in the rate of extraction. It is not the date the last unit of a resource disappears. Production depends on geology, technology, investment, prices and demand. The book includes forecasts made before publication in 2016. Treat their dates as historical predictions to evaluate—not as a schedule for the future. A useful question is, “Which assumptions would make this forecast change?”
Takeaway: energy security concerns include availability, access and demand, not simply the amount of material underground. Efficiency can reduce the energy needed for a service without discovering a new deposit.


9.5 Fossil fuel extraction and use can harm the environment
Follow each fuel from extraction to use. Surface mining removes overburden and can alter topography, drainage and habitats. Exposure of sulfide-bearing material can contribute to acidic drainage and mobilization of contaminants. Mountaintop removal can affect valleys and streams beyond the pit itself. Combustion adds air pollutants and carbon dioxide; captured pollutants and ash still need management. Reducing an air emission can create a residual material requiring safe handling rather than making the contaminant vanish.
Oil development adds wells, transport infrastructure, spills and processing burdens. Acute releases and chronic leakage create different exposure patterns. Oil-sands extraction illustrates why the footprint includes water, energy use and disturbed ecosystems, not only the final fuel. A barrel from one pathway cannot be assumed to have the same upstream impacts as a barrel from another.
For hydraulic fracturing, trace water acquisition → chemical mixing → injection → flowback → treatment or disposal. Potential impacts differ by stage. Wastewater-disposal injection is not the same operation as fracturing a production well; distinguish mechanisms when discussing induced seismicity. The chapter’s descriptions of studies and regulations reflect their historical context, not a current legal or regulatory assessment. [Book, pp. 277–281.]


When extraction changes the landscape





Mountaintop-removal mining in West Virginia. Photograph: Mary Hufford / Library of Congress, via USGS, public domain. A photograph shows disturbance; downstream effects require measurements as well.

Enlarge figure




The same region in 1987





Landsat 5, June 6, 1987. NASA / USGS. Compare with the 2011 view. Source: NASA Earth Observatory: mountaintop mining.

Enlarge figure



The same region in 2011





Landsat 5, June 8, 2011. NASA / USGS. Light disturbed areas have expanded. This visual comparison does not by itself quantify water quality or human exposure. NASA source.

Enlarge figure


Mini-investigation: choose an impact and identify a source, a transport pathway, an exposed receptor and a measurable response. For example, a change in mine drainage can affect downstream water chemistry and aquatic organisms. What upstream comparison or pre-extraction measurement would help evaluate that claim?


9.6 Nuclear power development comes with environmental costs
Nuclear electricity avoids fossil combustion at the reactor, but uranium extraction, fuel preparation, cooling and waste management remain part of its life cycle. The chapter’s uranium-mining case describes occupational and community concerns. Evidence concerning exposed miners should not be generalized automatically to everyone living in a region: exposure routes, duration and study populations matter.
Spent fuel requires management because it contains radioactive materials and produces heat. “Waste is small in volume” and “waste needs long-term stewardship” can both be true. Volume alone does not specify hazard, exposure or the effectiveness of containment. Nor does the disappearance of one parent isotope establish that all daughter products are harmless.
Three Mile Island, Chernobyl and Fukushima are distinct historical cases, with different reactor designs and accident sequences. Use them to ask about heat removal, barriers, human decisions and interacting hazards—not to treat every accident as the same mechanism. Fukushima especially connects loss of power and cooling with the need to manage heat after shutdown. [Book, pp. 281–284; NRC clarification linked above.]
Discussion: who receives the electricity, who lives near extraction or waste facilities, and who pays for stewardship after a plant stops generating? Environmental comparison includes the distribution and duration of burdens.

title: Chapter 9: Fossil Fuels and Nuclear Energy
text:
Solutions · Intervene, measure and revise

9.7 New laws and technology are cleaning up the oil industry
Prevention and response operate at different stages. Vessel protection, maintenance, inspection and preparedness address the probability or consequences of a spill. Once oil is released, booms can contain surface oil and skimmers can recover it, subject to weather, currents and oil properties. Recovered material must still be managed. The book discusses the Oil Pollution Act of 1990 as a historical response to spills; this lesson does not present its discussion as current legal guidance. [Book, pp. 284–286.]
Dispersants break oil into smaller droplets and redistribute it into the water column. That changes exposure pathways; it does not remove all oil or guarantee harmlessness. Compare this with physical recovery. A response can reduce one kind of exposure while increasing another, which is why site-specific assessment matters. See NOAA’s explanation of dispersants.


Response begins with an exposed organism





An oiled brown pelican is captured for cleaning following Deepwater Horizon (2010). Photograph: Tom MacKenzie / U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, public domain. Source agency. Rescue and rehabilitation address exposed wildlife; they do not replace spill prevention or ecosystem monitoring.

Enlarge figure


Oil-spill response room


Offline challenge: choose an intervention before a spill, during a surface spill near a sensitive shoreline, and after initial cleanup. Compare prevention, booms/skimmers, dispersants and ecological monitoring.




Debrief and offline solution

Before a spill, prioritize prevention and preparedness. During the stated surface-spill scenario, containment and recovery can address the immediate question when conditions permit. After response, monitor biological, water and sediment indicators against reference conditions. Dispersants are not synonymous with recovery, and a clean-looking surface is not proof of ecological restoration.




9.8 Ecosystem restoration can mitigate the environmental impacts of fossil fuel extraction
Restoration is more than covering bare ground. Recontouring land, conserving and replacing topsoil, reestablishing vegetation and monitoring water and soil conditions can restore important functions. The Powder River Basin example illustrates a planned sequence rather than a single act of reseeding. [Book, pp. 286–288.]
But vegetation cover, agricultural productivity, biodiversity and hydrological function are different endpoints. A site can improve on one while remaining far from its original state on another. Peatlands develop over very long timescales; planting trees cannot immediately recreate accumulated peat, its carbon stock or its water regulation. A reconstructed slope similarly does not automatically replace a buried stream or its ecological network.
Restoration jury: one team argues that a reclaimed site is successful because plant cover has recovered. Another requests evidence about native species, soils and drainage. Agree on three indicators, a reference condition and a monitoring period before judging success. Give credit for measurable criteria, not for choosing the most optimistic or pessimistic claim.


9.9 Advances in nuclear power plant operation and design are aimed at improving safety
Safety improvements combine prevention, detection, response and containment. Planning for interacting hazards matters: a flood can affect electrical equipment precisely when pumps and monitoring are needed. Backup systems must be evaluated for shared vulnerabilities, not merely counted.
Passive features use physical processes such as gravity or natural circulation to perform particular functions with less dependence on powered equipment. They reduce specified failure pathways; they do not imply that every conceivable accident is impossible. Simpler arrangements can help, but their performance must be assessed under defined conditions. [Book, pp. 288–291.]
The chapter also considers fuel reprocessing and fusion research. Reprocessing can recover usable material but brings additional processing, waste and security obligations. Fusion is a different nuclear pathway, not a synonym for an improved fission reactor. Project milestones and forecasts in this 2016 book should be identified as historical expectations, not treated as verified present-day deployment.

title: Chapter 9: Fossil Fuels and Nuclear Energy
text:
Chapter takeaways

Trace the mechanism: fossil combustion releases chemical energy; fission releases nuclear energy; both may feed a thermal electricity cycle.
Compare the same service: energy, power, efficiency, total use and per-person use are not interchangeable.
Follow the whole pathway: extraction, operation, cooling, residuals and closure all belong in the assessment.
Match solutions to causes: containment is not removal, shutdown is not immediate cooling, and vegetation cover is not complete ecosystem recovery.
Make a conditional recommendation: state who benefits, who bears a burden, what safeguard is proposed and what evidence would trigger a revision.

Answer the central question: we can reduce harm by using less energy for the same service, preventing releases, improving conversion and safety, restoring damaged functions and accepting continuing stewardship obligations. No single intervention removes every burden. A defensible choice makes the remaining burdens and uncertainties visible.
