title: Chapter 9: Fossil Fuels and Nuclear Energy
text:
Science: resources become services

Energy is an amount; power is a rate
A kilowatt-hour (kWh) measures energy. A kilowatt (kW) measures the rate of energy transfer. A 1 kW appliance operating for 2 hours uses 2 kWh. At larger scales, a generator delivering 100 MW steadily for 3 hours supplies 300 MWh.
\[
\text{Energy}=\text{power}\times\text{time}
\]
Coal, crude oil and uranium are primary resources. Electricity is an energy carrier. The service may be lighting, refrigeration, transportation or comfortable indoor temperatures. Providing the same service with less energy is an efficiency improvement.


Fossil fuels contain ancient chemical energy
Coal commonly originates in plant material accumulated in ancient wetlands. Burial, pressure and heat alter this material over geological time. Much petroleum originates in ancient aquatic organisms buried in sediments. Natural gas consists predominantly of methane and can occur with oil or coal or in other geological formations.
The original organisms captured energy through photosynthesis. Geological processes transformed their remains into concentrated fuels. These resources are nonrenewable because formation is much slower than consumption on human timescales.
Refining separates crude oil into fractions with different boiling ranges. Oil therefore supplies multiple products, including transport fuels, lubricants and chemical feedstocks. An electricity-only comparison does not describe every use of petroleum. [Textbook, pp. 265–269.]


Thermal generation converts heat into electricity
In a steam-cycle plant, heat produces steam, steam turns a turbine, and the turbine drives a generator. A condenser and cooling system remove rejected heat and allow the working fluid to circulate. Gas turbines can use hot combustion gases directly; combined-cycle plants also recover exhaust heat.
The book’s approximate 35% conversion efficiency supplies a useful classroom example:
\[
100\ \text{energy units in}=35\ \text{units of electricity}+65\ \text{units of heat}
\]
Energy does not disappear. Some leaves in forms that the plant cannot convert into useful electricity. This value is a teaching approximation from the text, not a universal performance claim about modern power plants. [Textbook, p. 271.]


Check your understanding: what happens with 200 input units?

At the same assumed efficiency, useful electricity is \(200\times0.35=70\) units. The remaining 130 units leave as heat. Efficiency describes this conversion; it does not measure every environmental impact.



Compare the same useful output
Comparing equal fuel inputs can hide a useful question: how much input is required to deliver 100 units of electricity?
At 35% efficiency, input is \(100/0.35\approx285.7\) units; rejected heat is approximately 185.7 units. At 40%, input is 250 and rejected heat is 150. The input reduction is \((285.7-250)/285.7\approx12.5\%\).
This is a comparison at equal service, not a claim that total environmental damage falls by 12.5%. That would require information about the fuels, extraction, emissions and affected ecosystems. Conservation tells us where energy goes; environmental assessment tells us why the pathway matters.

title: Chapter 9: Fossil Fuels and Nuclear Energy
section: Nuclear energy: a controlled chain reaction
text:
Nuclear energy: a controlled chain reaction

Nuclear fission supplies a different source of heat
Fission splits heavy atomic nuclei, releasing energy and neutrons. In a reactor, engineers control the chain reaction and transfer heat to a power cycle.
For a common water-moderated reactor:








Component
Function
Why it matters




Fuel
Contains fissile material
Supplies nuclear energy


Moderator
Slows neutrons
Affects the probability of subsequent fission


Control rods
Absorb neutrons
Regulate or stop the chain reaction


Coolant
Removes heat
Transfers energy and protects fuel


Containment
Provides a protective barrier
Limits potential releases



Designs vary, and water can serve as both moderator and coolant. Fission differs from fusion, which combines light nuclei. [Textbook, p. 273; NRC explanation.]
Shutdown does not mean immediate cooling. Radioactive fission products continue releasing decay heat. Cooling remains necessary after the chain reaction stops. The historical Fukushima case shows how loss of power and cooling can combine into a serious accident. Different reactor designs and accident sequences must not be treated as interchangeable. [Textbook, pp. 283, 289; NRC decay-heat glossary.]


Fission and radioactive decay are not the same process
In a chain reaction, neutrons from one fission can contribute to subsequent fissions. Neutron absorption helps control that chain. Radioactive decay is the spontaneous transformation of an unstable nucleus. Existing radioactive products do not stop transforming merely because the chain reaction has stopped.
For a single isotope, a half-life is the time over which the expected number of parent nuclei falls by one-half. It is not the time until all the material is gone. After one, two and three half-lives, the expected parent fractions are \(1/2\), \(1/4\) and \(1/8\). See the NRC definition of radiological half-life.

title: Chapter 9: Fossil Fuels and Nuclear Energy
section: Experiment 9.2: half-life is a repeated fraction
text:
Experiment 9.2: half-life is a repeated fraction
Question: If half the parent nuclei transform in one half-life, will the other half all transform in the next?
Predict. Begin with 256 imaginary parent nuclei and a four-model-year half-life. Predict the expected count at years 4, 8 and 12. Do not use subtraction by a constant amount; consider what “half of what remains” means.


Without JavaScript, halve 256 repeatedly: 256 → 128 → 64 → 32. The interactive model animates these expected counts and lets you change the half-life and elapsed time.


Investigate. Advance one half-life at a time. Then keep elapsed time at 8 model years and compare half-lives of 2, 4 and 8 model years. Record which variable you changed and which you held constant. Use the notebook below to explain the pattern.


Worked results and the important limitation

With a four-year half-life, expected counts are 128 at year 4, 64 at year 8 and 32 at year 12. At the same elapsed time of eight years, half-lives of 2, 4 and 8 years leave expected counts of 16, 64 and 128 respectively.
Individual nuclei decay randomly, so a real collection need not follow these exact integer counts. The display rounds an expected value to illustrate the pattern. Its invented isotope does not represent reactor fuel, a waste mixture or a safe handling interval. Daughter products may also be radioactive. Hazard depends on more than the fraction of original parents remaining.
The connection to shutdown is qualitative: radioactive transformation can continue after fission stops. Do not use this single-isotope curve as a reactor cooling or decay-heat prediction.

title: Chapter 9: Fossil Fuels and Nuclear Energy
text:
Issues: compare complete pathways
A fair comparison states what it includes: extraction, processing, transport, generation, delivery, waste and decommissioning. It also specifies the useful output being compared.








System
Climate pathway
Other important burdens




Coal
Carbon dioxide from combustion
Mining disturbance, air pollutants, ash and cooling water


Natural gas
Combustion CO₂ and upstream methane leakage
Water management, leakage and infrastructure


Nuclear
Low operational combustion emissions; upstream impacts still exist
Uranium extraction, cooling, radioactive waste and decommissioning



This table identifies mechanisms, not numerical rankings. Quantitative comparisons need consistent units, boundaries, locations and dates. [Textbook, pp. 277–289.]

An impact can move between places and forms
Coal extraction can change drainage, habitats and water chemistry. Capturing pollutants at a plant can move contaminants into ash or another residual stream requiring management. Oil spills can affect coastal ecosystems, but chronic releases also matter. Hydraulic fracturing involves water acquisition, chemical handling, injection, flowback, treatment and disposal; each stage creates potential exposure pathways.
A hazard is a potential source of harm. Risk depends on exposure, likelihood and consequences under particular conditions. Identifying a hazard is the beginning of an assessment, not a complete estimate of risk.


Build a source–pathway–receptor explanation
“Pollution is bad” identifies a concern but not a mechanism. A stronger explanation connects a source (for example, mine drainage), a pathway (movement through surface water), a receptor (an aquatic community or water user), and an effect that can be investigated. A safeguard should interrupt the pathway or reduce the source; monitoring should test whether it works.
Try the same structure for cooling-water discharge: thermal generation rejects heat, a water body may receive some of that heat, local conditions influence exposure, and temperature-sensitive organisms may be affected. The presence of a cooling system alone does not establish the size of that effect. You would need discharge characteristics, receiving-water conditions, biological evidence and a comparison condition.
Mini-investigation: choose one row in the comparison table. Write one source–pathway–receptor chain and name a measurement that could support or challenge it. Keep climate effects separate from local air or water effects; they do not have identical mechanisms or spatial scales.
Nuclear power adds the need to manage radioactive materials over appropriate timescales. The book’s uranium-mining discussion also illustrates unequal burdens on communities. Its evidence about miners should not be casually generalized to every nearby resident. [Textbook, pp. 277–283.]

title: Chapter 9: Fossil Fuels and Nuclear Energy
text:
Solutions: prevention and recovery
Oil-spill prevention, containment booms and skimmers act at different points in a release. Dispersants alter the distribution of oil and require their own impact assessment. None guarantees full restoration of the original ecosystem.
For mined land, replacing topsoil and establishing vegetation can restore functions. Yet productive grassland, original biodiversity and a reconstructed peat wetland are different outcomes. Define success before measuring it: water quality, native species, habitat connectivity, soil condition or a specified land use. The book contrasts restoration in the Powder River Basin with the difficulty of replacing slow-forming peat systems. [Textbook, pp. 285–287.]
For nuclear facilities, improvements include robust cooling, multiple protective barriers, planning for combined hazards, and passive systems that use physical processes such as gravity. These reduce risks without making every conceivable failure impossible. [Textbook, pp. 289–291.]

Classroom activity: Riverton’s energy decision
Fictional scenario. Riverton must replace an aging coal electricity contract in two years. Its council requires reliable service and wants lower pollution. The budget is 10 tokens. These tokens are invented constraints, not actual prices, emissions factors or technology rankings.
Work in teams of three or four. Assign an analyst, a community advocate and a spokesperson. Choose a plan and write the reasoning on paper.

Rules: select exactly one supply option (A, B or C), with optional D. Stay within 10 tokens. All three supply contracts initially meet the fictional service requirement. No option qualifies solely because it is cheapest.
Your recommendation must state:

The selected plan and token total.
One burden reduced and one retained.
Who receives benefits and who bears a remaining burden.
A safeguard and the evidence needed to evaluate it.



Stress card: reveal after the initial recommendation

The offered nuclear supply contract will not be available before the coal contract expires. This is a procurement delay in the fictional case, not a general nuclear construction-time assumption. Revise the sequence or justify a temporary bridge. Specify when and on what evidence the council should review the bridge.



Instructor guide and possible answers

A+D costs 6, B+D costs 8, and C+D costs 10. All satisfy the original budget. C+D can be defended as reducing operational fossil combustion while retaining uranium, cooling and waste obligations. It becomes unavailable by the deadline after the stress card. A temporary A+D or B+D plan can be defended only with acknowledged continuing burdens and a clear review condition. There is no unique numerical optimum because the exercise supplies no quantified environmental scores.
For a seminar activity, allow time to introduce the case, choose a plan, reveal the stress card, revise and compare recommendations. Extend the discussion as needed. The presentation has its own 50-minute timing.
Rubric, 8 points: correct mechanism (2), consistent comparison (2), affected community and safeguard (2), response to uncertainty and timing (2). Reward a defensible revision rather than loyalty to an initial answer.

title: Chapter 9: Fossil Fuels and Nuclear Energy
text:
Review and exit ticket



Is a visible cooling-tower plume a direct measure of CO₂ emissions?


No. The visible plume is generally condensed water droplets. Fuel use and measured emissions provide evidence about CO₂. A visual observation alone does not establish the emissions rate.




Why can a nuclear plant need cooling after shutdown?


Decay of radioactive fission products continues to produce heat after the chain reaction stops. Operators must continue removing that heat.




Does replanting a mine prove complete restoration?


No. The conclusion depends on the reference condition, the functions measured and the time allowed. Vegetation cover alone does not establish recovery of biodiversity or hydrology.

Final reflection: trace an energy pathway, explain one fossil–nuclear tradeoff, and name a measurement that could change your recommendation. Return to the chapter’s central question and revise your initial answer.

Explore ideas for engaging lectures and tools for visual mathematical learning. Open either resource below; each can be expanded independently.


Attention Span & Engagement in Long LecturesExplore the research, lecture breaks, games, quick quizzes & Q&A.


Teaching with attention in mind

Pause the lecture. Keep the learning moving.

Especially in lengthy lectures, plan opportunities to retrieve, discuss, ask, play, and rest. A quick quiz can reveal a misconception; a discussion can make reasoning visible; a genuine break can give students time away from the task. These activities serve different purposes—not one interchangeable “attention reset.”


What the evidence does—and does not—say. The familiar claim that everyone loses attention after 10–15 minutes has weak support. Attention varies with the learner, task and teaching context. Nor do the cited studies establish that every break restores attention to its maximum. Wilson & Korn (2007)
Two ways to understand the topic. Start with conceptual illustrations of re-engagement, then examine what researchers actually measured. Attention ratings, mind-wandering reports, performance and learning are related, but they are not interchangeable measures of “attention span.”


1. The teaching idea: attention, breaks, and re-engagement
Conceptual illustrations—not measured attention curves. A long stretch of listening can make attention harder to sustain. Purposeful changes of activity may help students re-engage; a genuine rest break offers time away from the task. Recovery need not be complete or the same after every interruption.

Understanding the “Learning Attention Span Curve”
A rest period uses time that could have been spent teaching, but renewed engagement afterward might compensate for that time. This original conceptual redraw explains the trade-off illustrated in Alix G. Darden’s faculty-development presentation.





Conceptual adaptation · not measured data. Original diagram informed by Alix G. Darden’s faculty-development presentation, slide 12, “Learning Attention Span Curve.” Layout, wording and curves have been redrawn; no data were extracted. View the source slide · Open the new figure full size.


How to read it: amber hatching represents the teaching opportunity set aside during rest; green shading represents a possible benefit afterward. The source calls these “learning loss” and “learning gain,” but neither shaded area quantifies learning. The dashed curve is a hypothetical comparison, not a measured control group. No performance is estimated during the rest period.
Use this as an explanation of why a pause may be worthwhile, not a prediction of recovery size or proof of a particular break schedule. The qualitative performance axis preserves the source’s distinction from a measured attention-span duration.


Continuous delivery and partial recoveries
Auckland’s paired diagrams illustrate a declining curve and progressively smaller rebounds. Their original vertical axis is “Level of performance,” not attention span. The timing and curve heights should not be read as measurements or an optimal break schedule. View Auckland’s teaching guidance.



One continuous stretch







Partial recoveries







Original graphics reproduced unchanged. © University of Auckland, Teaching large classes: Engaging your audience. Included for non-profit educational comparison; see the University’s copyright conditions.


Use the idea, not a stopwatch rule. Plan opportunities for a Quick Quiz (QQ), discussion, learning game, Q&A, or rest, and adjust the pace to students’ responses, task difficulty and accessibility needs. In shorter classes, choose fewer activities. Clarify confusion when it appears, even before a planned pause.
Keep the distinction clear: quizzes and discussions are active learning; they still require mental effort. Rest offers relief from academic work. Auckland cites Johnstone & Percival (1976) for its timing advice, but provides no dataset or methods establishing these exact curves or the effects of specific activities.




2. What researchers measured
These studies provide numerical observations. Each measures a different aspect of engagement, so their values should not be combined into a single universal attention curve.

Attention ratings across a 40-minute lecture
Farley, Risko, and Kingstone (2013) asked 21 students to rate their attention over each preceding five-minute interval. This plot uses the eight published means from Table 1, without smoothing or invented values. Read the study.





Measured results · redrawn from Table 1. Farley, Risko & Kingstone (2013), Frontiers in Psychology, 4:619. Points are group means; lines only connect adjacent intervals. Uncertainty intervals are not plotted. This small, self-report study does not establish a universal attention deadline.




View the published values and measurement scale

Ratings range from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree) with the statement “My attention is fully focused on the video.” Each rating summarizes the preceding interval, not one instant.

Finding: mean attention ratings rose initially, then generally declined from 6.3 in the second interval to 4.9 in the last.
Teaching implication: check engagement throughout a lecture rather than assuming it stays constant.
Limitation: 21 students rated their own attention during one video lecture. There was no comparison of break schedules, and the results do not identify a universal attention deadline.



Quizzes versus restudy between lecture segments
Welhaf et al. (2022) studied 195 students watching a roughly 50-minute statistics lecture. This is their original Figure 4, comparing mind-wandering reports across five blocks, with testing or restudy between segments. Read the study.





Published figure · reproduced unchanged. Welhaf, Phillips, Smeekens, Miyake & Kane (2022), Figure 4, Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications, 7:26. © The authors, CC BY 4.0. Open full-size figure.



How to read it: TUT means task-unrelated thought; lower is better. Blue represents restudy, orange represents testing. Small dots show students’ rates, larger filled/open circles show means, and bars are 95% confidence intervals. The shaded shapes show the distributions.
Finding: testing modestly reduced overall mind-wandering compared with restudy.
Teaching implication: the activity between lecture segments may matter, not just the interruption itself.
Limitation: evidence was mixed across statistical approaches. The study did not establish different time-course trajectories or repeated recovery after each interruption. Both groups had activities between segments; this was not a breaks-versus-no-breaks comparison.



Why include quick quizzes?
Szpunar, Khan, and Schacter studied a 21-minute statistics video. In Experiment 2, participants receiving interpolated tests reported less mind wandering than the comparison groups. All groups had interruptions: this was not simply “breaks versus no breaks.” Read the paper and Figure 2B.





Original plot of reported group means. Self-reported mind wandering is not an attention-span duration. This small video-lecture experiment does not validate the conceptual curves above.



Finding: Experiment 2’s reported mind-wandering means were 19% with interim quizzes, 39% with restudy, and 41% without interim quizzes.
Teaching implication: ask students to recall an idea before displaying its answer. A low-stakes quiz can serve this purpose during a lecture.
Limitation: this experiment included 48 participants watching a 21-minute video. The percentages summarize thought-probe reports, not percentages of inattentive students or measured attention-span durations. The results do not establish recovery after every kind of break.


On a small screen, swipe a wide plot sideways to read it completely. The chart regions also support keyboard scrolling.




Choose the interruption for the learning purpose



Quick Quiz · retrieve


Ask one low-stakes question before showing the answer. Let everyone respond individually, then explain the reasoning. Use the pattern of answers to decide whether to continue or reteach.




Discussion · explain


Give a concrete prompt: “Which explanation fits, and why?” Include quiet thinking time, pair discussion, then a short debrief. Offer a written alternative to speaking aloud.




Learning game · apply


Try a prediction challenge, concept match, or “spot the error.” Tie the game to a course objective. Reward reasoning and feedback, not speed alone; avoid mandatory public rankings.




Q&A · diagnose


Collect questions throughout the lecture, including anonymous or written submissions. Ask students to name the least clear step instead of relying only on “Any questions?”




Rest break · recover


Make this a genuine pause from academic work. Offer water, quiet rest, or optional movement without requiring standing. A quiz or discussion is active learning, not necessarily rest.




Re-entry · reconnect


State the question the next segment will answer, connect it to the preceding activity, and check understanding. A lively room is not by itself evidence that everyone has learned.



These are practical teaching suggestions, not experimentally established effect sizes for each activity. A large STEM meta-analysis supports active learning for achievement, but does not supply minute-by-minute attention curves or prove that every game or Q&A format works equally well. Freeman et al. (2014)
For genuine rest, a meta-analysis found small benefits of micro-breaks for vigor and fatigue; the overall performance effect was not statistically significant. Its work-task evidence is not a direct estimate of classroom attention recovery. Albulescu et al. (2022)


Research and teaching sources: how they are used here


Wilson, K., & Korn, J. H. (2007). Attention during lectures: Beyond ten minutes. Teaching of Psychology, 34(2), 85–89. DOI: 10.1080/00986280701291291. Review informing the caution against a universal attention deadline.
Szpunar, K. K., Khan, N. Y., & Schacter, D. L. (2013). Interpolated memory tests reduce mind wandering and improve learning of online lectures. PNAS, 110(16), 6313–6317. DOI: 10.1073/pnas.1221764110. Source for the empirical bar chart, not for the conceptual curves.
Freeman, S., et al. (2014). Active learning increases student performance in science, engineering, and mathematics. PNAS, 111(23), 8410–8415. DOI: 10.1073/pnas.1319030111. Meta-analysis of achievement and failure outcomes, not attention duration.
Albulescu, P., et al. (2022). “Give me a break!” A systematic review and meta-analysis on the efficacy of micro-breaks for increasing well-being and performance. PLOS ONE, 17(8), e0272460. DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0272460. Evidence about recovery between tasks; distinct from instructional activities.
Farley, J., Risko, E. F., & Kingstone, A. (2013). Everyday attention and lecture retention: the effects of time, fidgeting, and mind wandering. Frontiers in Psychology, 4:619. DOI: 10.3389/fpsyg.2013.00619. Table 1 supplies the attention-rating means and standard deviations used above.
Welhaf, M. S., Phillips, N. E., Smeekens, B. A., Miyake, A., & Kane, M. J. (2022). Interpolated testing and content pretesting as interventions to reduce task-unrelated thoughts during a video lecture. Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications, 7:26. DOI: 10.1186/s41235-022-00372-y. Original Figure 4 reproduced under CC BY 4.0; no changes.
University of Auckland. Teaching large classes: Engaging your audience. Teaching guidance, not a peer-reviewed study; source of the unchanged conceptual diagrams. Its timing advice cites Johnstone, A. H., & Percival, F. (1976), Attention breaks in lectures, Education in Chemistry, 13, 49–50; the diagrams’ exact curves are not verified measurements here.
Darden, A. G. The Intersection of Research and Teaching, faculty-development presentation, slide 12, “Learning Attention Span Curve.” Source of the rest-versus-teaching-time idea in our original conceptual adaptation. Layout, labels and curves are redrawn; no measured data are implied. The source slide remains linked for comparison.

Using the observatory


Explore the constellation
Choose from 12 missions, including the ISS, Sentinel, Landsat, SMAP, GPM Core, Aqua, and GOES-18. Select a mission from the catalog or the phone’s dropdown. Open Mission details on a small screen to see its altitude, speed, and orbital data.
Use Earth view for nearby orbits and GEO scale to appreciate the distance to geostationary orbit. Spacecraft symbols are enlarged for visibility; Earth and orbit distances use the same scale.
Use + / −, pinch, or scroll to zoom. Explore land opens a coordinate navigator and a Fayetteville, Arkansas example. As you approach the surface, progressively finer 2024 Sentinel-2 imagery loads from EOX. At the finest scale, land detail is approximately 10 m—useful for landscapes and fields, not street-level photography. The close-up view follows Earth’s rotation and uses daylight imagery for visibility, independent of the simulation’s day/night cycle. Earth view returns to the orbital overview.


Control time and motion
Pause the simulation, follow a spacecraft, or accelerate time from 1× to 1000×. Live now returns the simulation clock to the current time; it does not turn predicted positions into live measurements.
Toggle orbits, ground tracks, labels, and the geometric horizon. The horizon ring is not a sensor’s imaging footprint. Reduced-motion preferences start the viewer paused.

Model assumptions, data updates, and credits


What the model includes
The viewer uses satellite.js 6.0.1 for SGP4/SDP4 orbital propagation and Three.js 0.170.0 for rendering. Earth rotation follows Greenwich sidereal time. Earth is displayed as a sphere of radius 6,378.137 km. The Sun direction is approximate and intended for illustrative lighting, not precision eclipse analysis.
The visibility calculator samples at 30-second intervals. It assumes sea-level elevation and an unobstructed horizon; it does not model terrain, atmospheric refraction, or instrument scheduling. Old orbital elements and spacecraft maneuvers can reduce prediction accuracy. This is an educational and exploratory tool, not an operational tracking service.


Orbital-data updates
A bundled orbital snapshot lets the tool start even if the external data service is unavailable. Elements checks the public TLE API for updates; successful checks are cached in your browser for two hours. Failed checks retain existing elements. Data-age warnings are reminders to check the source, not quantified accuracy guarantees.


Surface imagery
The orbital overview uses the bundled NASA-based globe. Close-up views stream visible tiles from EOxCloudless, a static Sentinel-2 mosaic with approximately 10 m source resolution. The viewer does not model terrain relief or buildings. Clarity and coverage vary; oceans and polar areas may have less detail. When the imagery service fails or has no coverage, the lower-resolution globe remains available. View height is a camera distance above the spherical Earth, not an imagery resolution measurement.
EOX provides these tiles free for non-commercial use with attribution, under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 for 2024 imagery. Attribution stays on the map. No API key or paid AI service is used. Tile requests reveal the viewed region and normal connection information to EOX; this is separate from the research-site calculator, whose calculations remain local. The viewer limits simultaneous requests and keeps a bounded in-memory cache rather than downloading the world.


Distance to the surface below
The optional overlay uses the predicted satellite position, Copernicus GLO-90 surface elevations through Open-Meteo, and a local EGM2008 geoid correction. It estimates distance along the local reference-ellipsoid normal, not the shortest distance to an off-axis mountain or an individual object. Ocean distances refer to the modeled water surface, not the seabed. Negative elevations are retained; zero elevation is not treated as proof of ocean.
The calculation is satellite ellipsoid height − (surface elevation + geoid correction), with all terms converted to kilometres. Both heights belong to the same sampled time and location; the viewer does not combine a new satellite position with old terrain. Readings more than 15 simulated seconds old are hidden. Higher terrain reduces the distance at the same orbital height, but orbital variation means oceans do not necessarily produce the maximum distance.
The static terrain grid has approximately 90 m horizontal sampling. The local geoid is a 0.5° subsample of the public-domain NGA EGM2008 model distributed by PROJ; generation metadata and validation are available. Neither this grid nor the orbital prediction supports survey-grade accuracy. Fine peaks, individual objects, waves, tides and terrain changes are not resolved reliably; tenths of a kilometre are display precision, not a guaranteed error bound. The globe remains visually spherical.
Enabling the option sends predicted satellite ground coordinates—not your device location—to Open-Meteo, at most one batch every five seconds. Requests stop when disabled, fast-forwarding or the tab is hidden; paused, already-sampled positions reuse cached elevations. The free non-commercial service has rate limits and no availability guarantee. Missing data produce Unavailable, never a fabricated zero-height surface.
